Home of the new NeuralFoil, built from the completed validation study

NeuralFoil Studio

This site now ships NeuralFoil B, the new NeuralFoil: the same eight shipped networks wrapped in the study's measured trust map, so every force and moment coefficient arrives with its 8-network disagreement band and a plain-language verdict on whether to trust it. The New NeuralFoil tab is the tool; New vs Classic shows exactly what changed, what honestly could not be fixed, and the measurements behind both. Everything below it is the full Studio, unchanged: a simulation workbench with NeuralFoil itself inside: the actual 0.3.3 network runs live in this page, so every one of the 1,655 UIUC airfoils gets full polars, pressure distributions, transition, confidence, and a data-matched viscous flow field; recalibrate the transonic wave-drag layer with the study's three pre-registered parameters; verify everything on the Checks tab; and export publication-ready figures and movies.

Sixty-second tour

New NeuralFoil is the flagship: pick any airfoil and condition and get lift, drag and moment with their 8-network disagreement bands and a trust verdict from the study's measured failure map, including Mach effects the classic confidence score cannot see. New vs Classic shows the live difference between the new release and classic NeuralFoil 0.3.3, the measured evidence for every change, and the honest list of what could not be fixed. Flow shows air moving over the airfoil: in viscous mode a field matched to the run's surface velocities with a computed boundary layer, separation marks, and a wake carrying the run's drag; the search bar up top swaps in any of 1,655 real airfoils, and each one gets a full NeuralFoil run computed live by the actual network, ported into this page and verified on the Checks tab. 3D view extrudes the same solution into an orbitable wing. Polars holds the six performance charts. Pressure & transition shows the pressure distribution and where the boundary layer trips. Transonic lab is the study's recalibration playground with its three pre-registered parameters. Model sizes compares all eight NeuralFoil networks by speed and accuracy. Geometry is an exact NACA shape designer. Compare puts any two airfoils side by side: shapes, live lift curves, pressure distributions, and full geometry statistics. Flight lab puts the section in real air with the standard atmosphere: dimensional forces, stall speed, and a glider speed polar. Checks audits the data and the solver against classical theory, including an exact-solution verification. Digitizer turns a scanned wind-tunnel chart into data points you can fit. Movie maker records any of it as video. Every chart exports as a white, print-ready PNG with its caption attached, and the arrow keys nudge α.

Air over the airfoil, live

The wing in three dimensions

Drag to orbit the wing. What you are seeing, precisely: the current airfoil's two-dimensional solution extruded along the span of an untwisted, unswept, constant-chord wing, carrying every layer of the Flow tab. The surface is colored by the run's real pressure distribution (or shown as plain material with the toggle), the translucent sheet over it is the same Thwaites/Head boundary layer with its thickness exaggeration, the slab behind is the wake whose momentum deficit equals the run's drag, and the dark lines across the span mark stagnation, transition, and (dashed) predicted separation. Particles follow the two-dimensional velocity field at every span station, slowed by the real viscous field near the surface and in the wake, which is exactly the assumption behind section analysis. The pressure-field toggle draws the computed Cp field as one continuous translucent volume enveloping the whole wing, and the stream-surfaces toggle draws each streamline as a continuous sheet flowing tip to tip; under the 2D assumption the field is identical at every span station, so both are exact extrusions of the Flow tab's solution, not interpolations. While you orbit or the airfoil moves, both render at reduced detail and sharpen the moment the motion settles. The rounded tips are a geometric fairing only. True three-dimensional effects, tip vortices and downwash, are not simulated in this picture; the Flight lab accounts for them in its labeled induced-drag estimate.

Experimental residuals

After a fit, the bootstrap answers the question a reviewer will ask: how much do the three fitted parameters wobble if your data had come out slightly differently? It resamples your points with replacement, refits each time, and reports the middle 95 percent. The intervals describe fit stability under resampling, nothing more.

The three sliders are exactly the three free parameters pre-registered in the Methods: the leading coefficient, the exponent, and an offset between predicted critical Mach and the Mach where measured drag rise begins. The shipped curve is CD,wave = 80(M − Mcrit)⁴ from the current AeroSandbox analysis path; the critical Mach number comes from Eq. 8 of the NeuralFoil paper applied to the real suction peak of the selected operating point. In Phase B, digitized wind-tunnel points take the place of your fingers on these sliders.

Flight lab: the section in real air

Glider speed polar

At the working point

What is real here: the section CL, CD, and CM at every angle are the run's genuine NeuralFoil results, and the atmosphere is the International Standard Atmosphere with Sutherland viscosity, computed exactly. What is an estimate, and labeled as one: the finite-wing correction is the classic lifting-line result CDi = CL²/(π·AR·e) for a rectangular wing, a textbook formula, not a 3D simulation. Each level-flight speed follows from lift equals weight. The section data comes from the toolbar's selected Reynolds sweep; the readout shows the actual flight Reynolds number so you can judge the match yourself, and warns when they differ badly. Available for AG04, the airfoil with a measured run.

This tab audits the active run (AG04's precomputed reference run, or the live-computed run of any other selected airfoil) against classical aerodynamics, computed live in this page. Disagreement is shown, never blended: each chart says which method produced which curve, and the gaps themselves are informative. These are the same kinds of internal-consistency checks the study's validity map runs at scale.

Ported-network verification

The NeuralFoil network in this page is the exact nn-xlarge weight file from version 0.3.3. This check runs AG04 through the ported network at all 846 conditions of the reference run and reports the largest differences. Residuals at the fourth decimal are expected: the stored reference coordinates are rounded to five decimals, and that rounding alone moves CL by more than the port's largest error.

Drag closure: Squire-Young vs the run

The classical chain here is Thwaites' laminar method, transition at the run's own reported location, Head's turbulent method, and the Squire-Young formula CD = 2·(θ/c)·(ue/U∞)(H+5)/2 at the trailing edge, summed over both surfaces. It is fed by the run's real edge velocities, so this asks a precise question: is the drag NeuralFoil reports consistent with the pressures and transition it reports, judged by the standard integral method? Agreement within the method's own error band (roughly 10 to 20 percent in its classical applications) is a pass.

Lift bookkeeping: pressure integration vs the run

Trapezoid integration of the run's own 32-point pressure distributions into a normal-force coefficient, rotated to lift. Pure arithmetic on the dataset, no new physics. The residual has two known, named sources: 32-point quadrature truncation (the suction peak is sharper than the grid), and the excluded chordwise force component. A residual that stays small and smooth means the published coefficients and the published pressure distributions tell one consistent story.

Solver verification: the Joukowski exact solution

The Hess-Smith solver behind every live flow in this app, tested against a case with a known exact answer: a Joukowski airfoil, whose full pressure field follows in closed form from the conformal map.

Surface pressure: exact vs panel

Convergence with panel count

This is the standard verification a reviewer expects of any solver: compare against an exact solution and show the error shrink as resolution grows. The Joukowski trailing edge is a cusp, the hardest case for a panel method, so this is a conservative test; the airfoils in the library all have finite trailing-edge angles, which the solver handles more easily.

Transition: Michel's correlation vs the run

Michel's criterion (Reθ ≥ 1.174·(1 + 22400/Rex)·Rex0.46) evaluated live along a Thwaites laminar march driven by the run's real edge velocities, against the transition locations the run reports. NeuralFoil inherits XFOIL's eN amplification method, a fundamentally richer model than this one-line correlation, so systematic offsets are expected and interpretable rather than alarming; what matters is that the two move together as α and Re change.

Plot digitizer: turn a scanned wind-tunnel chart into data

The study's Phase B needs numbers out of published wind-tunnel figures. Load a chart image (a screenshot or scan of a CD-versus-Mach plot), calibrate the axes with four clicks, then click each data point. Your clicks become a CSV, or go straight into the Transonic lab as experimental points. Calibration handles a slightly rotated scan; every value here is your own reading of the source figure.

No image loaded.

Steps: set the four reference values to match numbers printed on the chart's axes, press each "click it" and then click that reference on the image (two points on the x axis, two on the y axis). After calibration, every click on the image adds a data point; a magnifier follows your cursor for precision. For the lab, digitize Mach on x and drag coefficient on y (absolute CD or drag counts both work; the lab auto-detects). Axes are assumed linear, which matches the classic NACA drag-rise figures.

Movie maker

Pick a scene, then record, and keep this tab visible while it runs (browsers slow hidden tabs). Movies use the toolbar's Reynolds number; the Mach ramp also uses the current α and the Transonic lab sliders.

Movies render on a white background at 1280×720 and save as .webm, which plays in browsers and drops into PowerPoint or Google Slides. Like everything here, they animate the real precomputed sweep and the published formulas; no new physics is invented between frames.

What is real on this page

Every aerodynamic number in the Polars, Pressure, and Model sizes tabs, and every suction peak feeding the Transonic lab, is a genuine NeuralFoil result from a precomputed run: . That run produced 846 analyses (141 angles of attack × 6 Reynolds numbers) with full 32-point pressure distributions, transition locations, and pitching moments, plus an 8-way model-size comparison at Re 500k. This page performs no aerodynamic prediction of its own.

What is computed live

Three things, all from published formulas: the critical Mach number, via Eq. 8 of Sharpe & Hansman (2025), applied to the run's real minimum pressure coefficients; the shipped wave-drag layer, CD,wave = 80(M − Mcrit)⁴, as implemented in the current AeroSandbox analysis path; and exact NACA four-digit geometry in the Geometry tab. Derived arithmetic (glide ratio, drag counts, model-size differences) is labeled where it appears.

Motion between two settings is visual easing between real computed states: neighboring 0.25° samples of the run, or the two Reynolds sweeps being switched. Readouts and exported figures always land exactly on the computed values.

Movies

The Movie maker tab records .webm animations of the same data: the α sweep with its live pressure distribution, the working point tracing the polars, or a Mach ramp climbing the wave-drag curve. Frames render on a white background, sized for slides and supplementary material. Figure exports are also always white, whatever the screen theme, because the paper prints on white.

Experimental data and the fit

The Transonic lab accepts your digitized wind-tunnel points as CSV, plots them on the wave-drag chart, and can run the study's pre-registered three-parameter fit (leading coefficient, exponent, onset offset) against them with a robust soft-L1 loss, reporting the error before and after in drag counts. Points you load are your data; the fit is exactly the calculation Phase B pre-registers.

The airfoil library and the ported network

The search bar carries the UIUC Airfoil Coordinate Database: 1,655 real airfoil geometries, the standard public archive of nearly every airfoil design in wide circulation, each with its computed thickness and camber values. Selecting one rebuilds the panel solver for its true coordinates, and, since the network release, also computes a full NeuralFoil run for it on the spot: this page embeds the actual nn-xlarge weight tensors from NeuralFoil 0.3.3 (Sharpe, MIT license) and evaluates them exactly as the Python package does, including the airfoil normalization, the CST least-squares fit, the flipped-evaluation symmetry averaging, and the Mahalanobis confidence penalty. The port is verified on the Checks tab against the AG04 reference run at all 846 conditions; the largest difference is a few thousandths of CL, attributable to the five-decimal rounding of the stored reference coordinates. All NeuralFoil limitations apply unchanged to these live runs, which is exactly what the study characterizes. The analysis-conditions panel under the toolbar exposes the network's own remaining inputs, the n_crit transition criterion and forced boundary-layer trips, and any non-default setting recomputes the active run live, AG04 included. The Geometry tab can analyze a NACA design you shape yourself and sweep a whole thickness or camber family through the network, the study's original question run as an in-page experiment; and any run, live or reference, exports as JSON in the same format gen_dataset.py produces.

The Compare and Flight tabs

The Compare tab is exact geometry plus live inviscid panel solutions: outlines to scale, computed leading-edge radius, trailing-edge angle and cross-section area, lift curves and pressure distributions solved from the true coordinates, and lift slope and zero-lift angle fitted to those solutions. The Flight lab combines three honest ingredients: the run's real section coefficients, the International Standard Atmosphere with Sutherland viscosity (exact published formulas), and the classic lifting-line induced-drag estimate CDi = CL²/(π·AR·e), which is labeled as the textbook approximation it is. The speed polar solves lift equals weight at every angle of the real sweep. The boundary-layer profile you can open in the Flow view is reconstructed from the computed integral parameters through the standard Pohlhausen and power-law profile families, and says so on the plot.

The Checks tab and the correction ensemble

The Checks tab audits the dataset with classical methods computed live: Squire-Young drag closure through the Thwaites/Head march, trapezoid pressure-integration of lift, and Michel's transition correlation, each plotted unblended against the run's own values. The Reynolds-scaling chart in Polars brackets the six real drag points with the published laminar (Blasius) and turbulent (Schlichting) flat-plate anchors. And the Transonic lab's correction ensemble applies three published compressibility rules (Prandtl-Glauert, Karman-Tsien, Laitone) to the same real suction peak and reports the spread of critical Mach numbers they imply, next to Eq. 8's closed-form value; that spread is disagreement between published rules, not uncertainty in the flow, and it is exactly the model-form question the paper's recalibration addresses.

Verification and uncertainty

The Checks tab can verify the page's own solver against the closed-form Joukowski exact solution, with a panel-count convergence study, the standard evidence that a numerical method is implemented correctly. When experimental points are loaded, the Transonic lab shows per-point residuals against both models, and a residual bootstrap refits the three parameters across 400 resamples of your data to report 95 percent intervals and a curve envelope; those intervals describe the stability of the fit under resampling of your points, and nothing else. The Pressure tab's Mach slider applies the published Karman-Tsien correction pointwise to the run's real incompressible pressures and shades where the corrected flow would be locally supersonic; the correction is a published formula, the shading follows from it, and the incompressible data underneath is untouched. Airfoil search accepts thickness and camber filters such as t<8 or c>2 alongside names, hovering any result previews its shape and extended geometry, and the top row of the dropdown (or dropping a file anywhere on the page) loads your own Selig or Lednicer .dat coordinate file as the working airfoil, live run included.

The Digitizer and the validity map

The Digitizer tab converts a loaded chart image into numbers through your own clicks: a four-point axis calibration (tolerant of a slightly rotated scan) followed by one click per data point, with a magnifier for precision. Nothing is inferred from the image automatically; every value is your reading of the source figure, which is exactly how the study's digitization step is defined in the Methods. The validity-map card in Polars shows NeuralFoil's self-reported confidence over the entire grid of the run, 141 angles by six Reynolds numbers, which is the at-a-glance version of the region map the paper's Phase A audits against experiment.

The flow view

The Flow tab and the flow movie do run a real solver: the classical Hess-Smith panel method, implemented in this page and solved from the airfoil geometry with the Kutta condition each time α changes. It is the standard first-principles method for inviscid, incompressible flow, so it is exact about what it models and silent about what it does not: no boundary layer, no separation, no stall. It is shown for intuition and for an honest comparison against the viscous NeuralFoil results (the Pressure tab can overlay both), and it never feeds any number reported as a NeuralFoil prediction.

What this page is for

AG04 is a low-Reynolds glider airfoil; it never flies near Mach 1. Applying the transonic layer to its suction peaks demonstrates the pipeline the study recalibrates, not a claim about AG04. The study itself runs the same pipeline on NACA sections and judges it against historical wind-tunnel measurements, with airfoil families held out of the fit. Watch the confidence badge as you sweep to the edges of the data: where the predictions misbehave, the score drops. Auditing exactly that behavior against experiment is one of the paper's contributions.
